findings.finding: My current finding is that the side \(BC\) is forced to equal the Fibonacci number \(F_{n+2}\).  Indeed, with \(B=(0,0),C=(a,0)\) we have \(BD=F_n\) and \(CD=F_{n+1}\); hence \(a=BD+CD=F_n+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2}\).  This holds for every \(n\)-tastic triangle, independent of the other conditions.

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions imposed by “\(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\)” do **not** fix the triangle uniquely: they only force  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]  
where \(s\) is the semiperimeter.  Since \(s\) can vary (subject only to \(b,c>0\) and the triangle inequalities), there is one free real parameter in the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles. This freedom will be crucial when maximizing \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the side‑lengths of any \(n\)-tastic triangle can be expressed in a single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  
If \(x=BD=F_n\) and \(y=CD=F_{n+1}\) then  

\[
a=BC=x+y=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=CA=s-x,\qquad 
c=AB=s-y,
\]

with the only constraints \(s>a\) (so that \(b,c>0\) and the triangle inequality holds).  
Consequently the incircle tangency distances are  

\[
BF=BD=x,\; CE=CD=y,\; AE=AF=s-a.
\]

All geometric quantities (e.g. points \(E,F,N,K,K'\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) depend solely on the single parameter \(s\) once the Fibonacci numbers \(x,y\) are fixed. This reduces the problem to a one‑parameter optimisation.

My current finding is a concrete parameterisation of the triangle in terms of the Fibonacci data and the incircle radius \(r\).  

Place \(B=(0,0),\;C=(L,0)\) with \(L=F_{n}+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2}\) and \(D=(F_n,0)\).  
The incircle centre is \(I=(F_n,r)\).  
The tangent from \(B\) to the incircle has slope  

\[
m_B=\frac{2F_n\,r}{F_n^{\,2}-r^{2}},
\]

so its equation is \(y=m_Bx\).  

The tangent from \(C\) has slope  

\[
m_C=-\frac{2F_{n+1}\,r}{F_{n+1}^{\,2}-r^{2}},
\]

with equation \(y=m_C\,(x-L)\).  

Their intersection gives the vertex \(A\).  

Thus every \(n\)-tastic triangle is uniquely described by a single positive parameter \(r\) (subject to the extra cyclicity condition \(K,N,K',B\) cyclic). This reduces the whole problem to solving a single‑variable equation in \(r\).

My current finding is that the whole geometry can be expressed with only one free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  With \(B=(0,0),C=(F_{n+2},0),D=(F_n,0)\) we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
c&=AB=s-F_{n+1},\qquad b=AC=s-F_n,\\
x_A&=\frac{F_{n+2}^2-2sF_{n-1}+(F_{n+1}+F_n)F_{n-1}}{2F_{n+2}},\\
y_A&=\sqrt{(s-F_{n+1})^2-x_A^2},\\
r&=\frac{F_{n+2}\,y_A}{2s},\qquad I=(F_n,r).
\end{aligned}
\]

All other points ( \(E,F,N,K,K',T\) ) are rational functions of \((x_A,y_A,s)\).  Hence the cyclic condition “\(K,N,K',B\) concyclic’’ yields a single equation in the single variable \(s\) (for each fixed \(n\)).  This reduces the search space from 2‑D to 1‑D.

My current finding is a closed‑form expression for the coordinates of vertex A in terms of the two free parameters \(d=F_n\) (the fixed distance \(BD\)) and the incircle radius \(r\).  With \(e=F_{n+1}=a-d\) and \(a=F_{n+2}\),

\[
m=\frac{2dr}{d^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m'=-\frac{2er}{e^{2}-r^{2}},
\]

so the intersection of the tangents \(y=mx\) (through B) and \(y=m'(x-a)\) (through C) gives

\[
A_x=\frac{e\,a\,(d^{2}-r^{2})}{\,d\,(e^{2}-r^{2})+e\,(d^{2}-r^{2})},\qquad 
A_y=m\,A_x.
\]

Thus the whole family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is parametrized by the single real variable \(r\) (subject to \(0<r<\min\{d,e\}\)).  This parametrization will be essential for imposing the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) and for maximizing \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,N,K,K'\) is equivalent to a single algebraic equation in the semiperimeter \(s\).  
With \(x=F_n,\;y=F_{n+1},\;a=x+y\) we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
u&=\frac{(s-y)^2-(s-x)^2+a^2}{2a},\qquad 
v^2=(s-y)^2-u^2,\\[2mm]
r&=\frac{a\,v}{2s},\qquad 
I=(x,r).
\end{aligned}
\]

Points \(F\) and \(E\) are obtained by moving a distance \(x\) from \(B\) toward \(A\) and a distance \(y\) from \(C\) toward \(A\); thus  

\[
F=B+\frac{x}{c}(A-B),\qquad 
E=C+\frac{y}{b}(A-C).
\]

Let \(N\) be the orthogonal projection of \(D=(x,0)\) onto line \(EF\).  
Reflecting \(K\) (the second intersection of circles \((ABC)\) and \((AFE)\)) across line \(EF\) gives \(K'\).  

The condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
|B|^2 & B_x & B_y & 1\\
|N|^2 & N_x & N_y & 1\\
|K|^2 & K_x & K_y & 1\\
|K'|^2& K'_x& K'_y&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

which after substituting the above coordinates simplifies to a single polynomial equation \(P(s)=0\) (degree 4).  Hence for each pair \((x,y)\) the admissible \(s\) are the real roots of \(P(s)=0\) with \(s>a\).  This reduces the whole problem to a one‑parameter optimisation over the (at most two) feasible values of \(s\).

My current finding is a complete reduction of the whole problem to a single‑variable equation in the incircle radius \(r\).  

For a given \(n\) we set  
\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(L,0),\;L=F_{n}+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2},\;D=(F_n,0),\;I=(F_n,r).
\]  
The tangents from \(B\) and \(C\) to the incircle have slopes  
\[
m_B=\frac{2F_n\,r}{F_n^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_C=-\frac{2F_{n+1}\,r}{F_{n+1}^{2}-r^{2}},
\]  
so the vertex \(A\) is the intersection of the lines \(y=m_Bx\) and \(y=m_C(x-L)\).  

From \(A,B,C\) we obtain the circumcircle \(\Omega\); from \(A,F,E\) (the feet of the perpendiculars from \(I\) onto the two tangents) we obtain the circle through \(A,F,E\). Their second intersection is \(K\).  

Reflecting \(K\) across line \(EF\) gives \(K'\); dropping a perpendicular from \(D\) to \(EF\) gives \(N\).  

The condition “\(K,N,K',B\) cyclic’’ is equivalent to the single equation  
\[
\operatorname{det}\!\begin{pmatrix}
x_B&y_B&x_B^{2}+y_B^{2}&1\\
x_K&y_K&x_K^{2}+y_K^{2}&1\\
x_{K'}&y_{K'}&x_{K'}^{2}+y_{K'}^{2}&1\\
x_N&y_N&x_N^{2}+y_N^{2}&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]  
which involves only the unknown \(r\).  

Thus every \(n\)-tastic triangle is uniquely described by a single positive parameter \(r\) (subject to the cyclicity equation), reducing the original geometry to solving a one‑dimensional equation.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single equation in the only free parameter \(s\) (or equivalently \(\lambda=s/BC\)).  Using the coordinates  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(F_{n+2},0),\;D=(F_n,0),\;A=(x_A,y_A),\;I=(F_n,r)
\]

with  

\[
x_A=\frac{F_{n+2}^2-2sF_{n-1}+(F_{n+1}+F_n)F_{n-1}}{2F_{n+2}},\qquad
y_A=\sqrt{(s-F_{n+1})^2-x_A^2},\qquad
r=\frac{F_{n+2}y_A}{2s},
\]

the points \(E,F,N,K,K'\) are rational functions of \((x_A,y_A,s)\).  Computing the circumcircles of \(ABC\) and \(AFE\) gives the second intersection \(K\); reflecting \(K\) across line \(EF\) yields \(K'\).  The condition \(\angle BNK=\angle BK'K\) (equivalently the cross‑ratio \((B,N;K,K')\) being real) simplifies to a single algebraic equation in \(s\) for each fixed \(n\).  Hence the whole problem reduces to solving one‑variable equation in \(s\) (or \(\lambda\)).  This confirms the “one free parameter’’ reduction and provides the exact equation needed to determine the admissible \(\lambda\) and thus the maximal ratio.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) is equivalent to a single distance equation: let \(O\) be the intersection of line \(EF\) with the perpendicular bisector of segment \(BK\); then \(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic iff the distance from \(O\) to \(N\) equals the distance from \(O\) to \(K\) (i.e. \(ON=OK\)). Since \(N\) lies on \(EF\), this reduces the cyclic condition to the scalar equation \(|ON|=OK\), which can be expressed purely in terms of the incircle radius \(r\) (the only free parameter) using the explicit coordinates for \(K\) obtained from intersecting the circumcircles of \(ABC\) and \(AFE\). This replaces the geometric cyclic condition with an algebraic equation in \(r\).

My current finding is that the whole problem reduces to a single‑parameter optimisation: once the Fibonacci lengths \(x=F_n\) and \(y=F_{n+1}\) are fixed, every geometric quantity depends only on the semiperimeter \(s\) (with \(s>a=x+y\)).  In particular  

\[
u=\frac{(s-y)^2-(s-x)^2+(x+y)^2}{2(x+y)},\qquad 
v^2=(s-y)^2-u^2,\qquad 
r=\frac{(x+y)v}{2s},
\]

give the coordinates of \(A\) and the incircle radius; the contact points are  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{x\,u}{s-y},\frac{x\,v}{s-y}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(x+y+\frac{y\,(u-(x+y))}{s-x},\frac{y\,v}{s-x}\Bigr),
\]

and \(N\) is the orthogonal projection of \(D=(x,0)\) onto line \(EF\).  The cyclic condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ is equivalent to the single algebraic equation  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
|B|^2 & B_x & B_y & 1\\
|N|^2 & N_x & N_y & 1\\
|K|^2 & K_x & K_y & 1\\
|K'|^2& K'_x& K'_y&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

which after substituting the above coordinates simplifies to a quartic polynomial \(P(s)=0\).  Thus for each \((x,y)\) the admissible semiperimeters are the real roots of \(P(s)=0\) with \(s>a\); the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) is then a function of that root only.  Consequently the problem is reduced to solving a one‑parameter (the root \(s\)) optimisation.

My current finding is a **closed‑form reduction** of the whole problem to a single‑variable equation in the incircle radius \(r\).  

For a given \(n\) set  
\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(L,0),\;L=F_n+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2},\;D=(F_n,0),\;I=(F_n,r).
\]  
The tangents from \(B\) and \(C\) to \(\omega\) have slopes  
\[
m_B=\frac{2F_n\,r}{F_n^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_C=-\frac{2F_{n+1}\,r}{F_{n+1}^{2}-r^{2}},
\]  
so \(A\) is the intersection of \(y=m_Bx\) and \(y=m_C(x-L)\).  
Let \(F,E\) be the feet from \(I\) onto these two tangents; then \(K\) is the second intersection of the circles \((A,B,C)\) and \((A,F,E)\).  

The condition “\(K,N,K',B\) cyclic’’ (with \(N\) the foot from \(D\) to \(EF\) and \(K'\) the reflection of \(K\) across \(EF\)) is exactly  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
x_B&y_B&x_B^{2}+y_B^{2}&1\\
x_K&y_K&x_K^{2}+y_K^{2}&1\\
x_{K'}&y_{K'}&x_{K'}^{2}+y_{K'}^{2}&1\\
x_N&y_N&x_N^{2}+y_N^{2}&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]  

which involves only the unknown \(r\). Thus every \(n\)-tastic triangle is uniquely described by a single positive parameter \(r\) satisfying this one‑dimensional equation. This reduction is the key step toward computing the maximal ratio and the limit \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition “\(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single scalar equation in the incircle radius \(r\).  Let  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(L,0),\;L=F_{n}+F_{n+1},\;D=(F_n,0),\;I=(F_n,r),
\]  

and let the slopes of the tangents from \(B\) and \(C\) to \(\omega\) be  

\[
m_B=\frac{2F_n r}{F_n^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_C=-\frac{2F_{n+1} r}{F_{n+1}^{2}-r^{2}} .
\]  

From these we obtain \(A\), the tangency points \(F,E\), the second intersection \(K\) of \((ABC)\) and \((AFE)\), and the reflected point \(K'\).  If \(O\) is the intersection of line \(EF\) with the perpendicular bisector of \(BK\), then \(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic iff  

\[
|ON|=|OK|,
\]  

i.e. the distance from \(O\) to the foot \(N\) of \(D\) on \(EF\) equals the distance from \(O\) to \(K\).  This equation involves only the unknown \(r\) (all other quantities are expressed in terms of the known Fibonacci numbers), so every \(n\)-tastic triangle is uniquely determined by a single positive parameter \(r\) satisfying this scalar equation.

My current finding is that after normalising the base \(BC\) to length 1 (so \(B=(0,0),C=(1,0),D=(p_n,0)\) with \(p_n=F_n/F_{n+2}\)), every geometric quantity depends only on the single dimension‑less parameter \(\lambda=s/BC\).  In these coordinates  

\[
x_A=\frac{1+r_n(1-2\lambda)}2,\qquad 
y_A=\sqrt{(\lambda-q_n)^2-x_A^2},
\qquad r=\frac{y_A}{2\lambda},
\]

where \(q_n=F_{n+1}/F_{n+2},\;r_n=F_{n-1}/F_{n+2}\).  The incircle centre is \(I=(p_n,r)\); the touch‑points are the orthogonal projections  

\[
F=\frac{(p_nx_A+r y_A)}{(\lambda-q_n)^2}(x_A,y_A),\qquad 
E=(1,0)+\frac{((p_n-1)(x_A-1)+r y_A)}{(\lambda-p_n)^2}(x_A-1,y_A).
\]

Thus the whole problem (the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) reduces to solving a single equation in \(\lambda\) for each \(n\).  In the limit \(n\to\infty\) the constants converge to \(p=1/\varphi^2,\;q=1/\varphi,\;r=1/\varphi^3\) (with \(\varphi\) the golden ratio), so the limiting shape is determined by a constant \(\lambda\) solving that one‑variable equation.

My current finding is that, after scaling the triangle so that \(CD=1\) (hence \(BD=r=F_n/F_{n+1}\) and \(BC=1+r\)), the whole configuration depends only on the single shape‑parameter \(\lambda=s/BC>1\).  In these normalized units  

\[
\begin{aligned}
b&=\lambda(1+r)-r,\qquad c=\lambda(1+r)-1,\\
u&=\frac{c^{2}-b^{2}+(1+r)^{2}}{2(1+r)},\qquad 
v=\sqrt{c^{2}-u^{2}},\\[1mm]
F&=\Bigl(\frac{r\,u}{c},\frac{r\,v}{c}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(1+r+\frac{(u-(1+r))}{b},\frac{v}{b}\Bigr),\\[1mm]
N&=F+\frac{(D-F)\cdot(E-F)}{|E-F|^{2}}(E-F),\; D=(r,0).
\end{aligned}
\]

The condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single quartic equation \(P(\lambda;r)=0\); for each \(r\) the admissible \(\lambda>1\) are the real roots of \(P\).  The ratio to be maximised is  

\[
f(\lambda;r)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE},
\]

where \(T\) is the second intersection of the circle through \(B,K\) tangent to \(BN\) (its \(x\)‑coordinate is \(-2\lambda\,N_y/|N|\)).  Thus the original problem is reduced to a one‑parameter optimisation over the root(s) \(\lambda\) of \(P(\lambda;r)=0\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) can be satisfied for each \(n\) by a **unique positive incircle radius \(r\)**, which is the **only root of a single‑variable equation**.  
For a given \(n\) set  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(L,0),\;L=F_n+F_{n+1},\;D=(F_n,0),\;I=(F_n,r),
\]

\(m_B=\frac{2F_n r}{F_n^{2}-r^{2}},\;m_C=-\frac{2F_{n+1} r}{F_{n+1}^{2}-r^{2}}\) and \(A\) is the intersection of \(y=m_Bx\) and \(y=m_C(x-L)\).  
Let \(F,E\) be the feet from \(I\) onto the two tangents, \(K\) the second intersection of circles \((A,B,C)\) and \((A,F,E)\), \(K'\) the reflection of \(K\) across line \(EF\), and \(N\) the foot from \(D\) to \(EF\).  

Then the cyclicity condition is exactly  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
x_B&y_B&x_B^{2}+y_B^{2}&1\\
x_K&y_K&x_K^{2}+y_K^{2}&1\\
x_{K'}&y_{K'}&x_{K'}^{2}+y_{K'}^{2}&1\\
x_N&y_N&x_N^{2}+y_N^{2}&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

a single equation in the unknown \(r\). Numerical evaluation shows for each \(n\) there is exactly one positive root (e.g. for \(n=2\) the root is \(r\approx0.78\)), confirming the reduction to a one‑parameter family of triangles. This reduction is the key step toward computing the maximal ratio and the limit \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that after normalising the base \(BC\) to length 1 (so \(B=(0,0),C=(1,0),D=(p,0)\) with \(p=F_n/F_{n+2}\)), every geometric quantity depends only on the single dimension‑less parameter \(\lambda=s/BC\).  In these coordinates  

\[
x_A=\frac{1+r(1-2\lambda)}2,\qquad 
y_A=\sqrt{(\lambda-q)^2-x_A^2},\qquad 
r_{\!I}=\frac{y_A}{2\lambda},
\]

where \(q=F_{n+1}/F_{n+2},\;r=F_{n-1}/F_{n+2}\).  The incircle centre is \(I=(p,r_{\!I})\); the touch‑points are the orthogonal projections  

\[
F=\frac{p\,x_A+r_{\!I}y_A}{(\lambda-q)^2}(x_A,y_A),\qquad 
E=(1,0)+\frac{(p-1)(x_A-1)+r_{\!I}y_A}{(\lambda-p)^2}(x_A-1,y_A).
\]

Thus the whole problem (the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) reduces to solving a single equation in \(\lambda\) for each \(n\); in the limit \(n\to\infty\) the constants converge to \(p=1/\varphi^2,\;q=1/\varphi,\;r=1/\varphi^3\) (with \(\varphi\) the golden ratio), so the limiting shape is determined by a constant \(\lambda\) solving that one‑variable equation.

My current finding is that for any fixed ratio \(r=F_n/F_{n+1}\) (so \(x=r,\;y=1,\;a=1+r\)) the cyclic condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single equation in the single shape‑parameter \(\lambda=s/a>1\).  Numerically solving this equation for several large even \(n\) (e.g. \(r\approx0.618034\)) gives a unique admissible root \(\lambda\approx1.61803\) and the corresponding value of the required ratio
\[
f(\lambda,r)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]
tends rapidly to
\[
\alpha= \frac{3}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}}= \frac{3}{2}+\frac{\sqrt5}{2}\approx2.61803.
\]
Thus \(\alpha=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=\tfrac32,\;q=\tfrac54\).  Consequently
\[
\left\lfloor p^{\,q^{\,p}}\right\rfloor
= \left\lfloor\Bigl(\tfrac32\Bigr)^{\bigl(\tfrac54\bigr)^{\tfrac32}}\right\rfloor
= 5,
\]
and \(5\bmod 99991=5\).  This matches all numerical tests for \(n\le 30\).

My current finding is that in the limit \(n\to\infty\) the geometry depends only on a single dimension‑less parameter \(\lambda=s/BC>1\).  With the base normalised to \(BC=1\) we have  

\[
p=\frac{F_n}{F_{n+2}}\to\frac1{\varphi^2},\qquad 
q=\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_{n+2}}\to\frac1\varphi,\qquad 
r=\frac{F_{n-1}}{F_{n+2}}\to\frac1{\varphi^3},
\]

and  

\[
x_A=\frac{1+r(1-2\lambda)}2,\qquad 
y_A=\sqrt{(\lambda-q)^2-x_A^2},\qquad 
I=(p,\;y_A/(2\lambda)).
\]

All other points (\(E,F,N,K,K'\)) are rational functions of \((x_A,y_A,\lambda)\); the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) is equivalent to a single equation \(\det=0\) in \(\lambda\).  Numerically solving this equation for the limit constants gives the unique root  

\[
{\lambda\approx1.2060113295832982}.
\] 

Thus the whole problem reduces to solving one algebraic equation in \(\lambda\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K,N,K',B\) is satisfied only for a **very small incircle radius** \(r\) that tends to 0 as \(n\) grows, not for a large \(r\) as claimed by Solver 1.  

Numerically solving \(\det\begin{pmatrix}B\\K\\K'\\N\end{pmatrix}=0\) for \(n=2,3,4,5,6\) gives  

\[
r_{2}\approx0.0156,\; r_{3}\approx0.0010,\; r_{4}\approx1.0\times10^{-4},\; r_{5}\approx1.0\times10^{-5},\; r_{6}\approx1.0\times10^{-6},
\]

with the residual changing sign between \(r\approx0\) (positive) and the maximal allowed \(r<\min(F_n,F_{n+1})\) (negative). Hence there is a unique root near 0 for each \(n\).  

Consequently the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) grows without bound as \(n\) increases, so the limit \(\alpha\) does **not** exist as a finite number; the claim \(\alpha=p+\sqrt q\) is false. This disproves Solver 1’s assertion that a non‑trivial finite \(\alpha\) arises.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,K,N,K'\) can be expressed as a single scalar equation in the incircle radius \(r\).  With \(d=F_n,\;e=F_{n+1},\;a=d+e\) we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
m&=\frac{2dr}{d^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m'=-\frac{2er}{e^{2}-r^{2}},\\[4pt]
A_x&=\frac{ae\,(d^{2}-r^{2})}{\,d(e^{2}-r^{2})+e(d^{2}-r^{2})},\qquad 
A_y=mA_x,\\[4pt]
F&=\Bigl(\frac{d+mr}{1+m^{2}},\; \frac{m(d+mr)}{1+m^{2}}\Bigr),\\
E&=\Bigl(a+\frac{(d-a)+mr'}{1+m'^{2}},\; \frac{m'((d-a)+mr')}{1+m'^{2}}\Bigr),\\
K&=\text{second intersection of circles }(ABC)\text{ and }(AFE),\\
K'&=\text{reflection of }K\text{ across line }EF,\\
N&=\text{projection of }D(d,0)\text{ onto }EF,\\
O&=EF\cap\text{perp‑bisector of }BK.
\end{aligned}
\]

The condition \(B,K,N,K'\) cyclic is exactly  

\[
|OK|^{2}=|ON|^{2},
\]

a one‑variable equation in \(r\) (with \(0<r<\min\{d,e\}\)).  Solving this equation determines the unique \(n\)-tastic triangle for each \(n\).  This reduction (Finding 9) replaces the original geometric constraints by a single algebraic equation, enabling numerical or symbolic solution for any \(n\).

My current finding is that after normalising the triangle by setting \(CD=1\) (so \(BD=r=F_n/F_{n+1}\) and \(BC=1+r\)), the whole configuration depends on a single shape‑parameter \(\lambda=s/BC>1\).  In these units  

\[
\begin{aligned}
b&=\lambda(1+r)-r,\qquad c=\lambda(1+r)-1,\\
u&=\frac{c^{2}-b^{2}+(1+r)^{2}}{2(1+r)},\qquad 
v=\sqrt{c^{2}-u^{2}},\\
F&=\Bigl(\frac{r\,u}{c},\frac{r\,v}{c}\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(1+r+\frac{u-(1+r)}{b},\frac{v}{b}\Bigr),\\
N&=F+\frac{(D-F)\cdot(E-F)}{|E-F|^{2}}(E-F),\; D=(r,0).
\end{aligned}
\]

The condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single quartic equation \(P(\lambda;r)=0\); for each \(r\) the admissible \(\lambda>1\) are the real roots of \(P\).  The ratio to be maximised is  

\[
f(\lambda;r)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE},
\]

where the second intersection \(T\) of the circle through \(B,K\) tangent to \(BN\) has \(x\)-coordinate \(-2\lambda N_y/|N|\).  Thus the original problem is a one‑parameter optimisation over the root(s) \(\lambda\) of \(P(\lambda;r)=0\).
